Great. Here’s a focused 3-week peaking block designed to taper volume, maintain/intensify effort, and leave the lifter fresh for meet day. It assumes access to a full gym (barbells, free weights, machines) and a 28-year-old female intermediate recreational lifter who has completed 12 weeks of accumulation and is prepping for a powerlifting meet in 21 days. The plan prioritizes squat, bench, and deadlift with competition-style setup, while preserving technique and addressing common peaking needs (auto-regulation, tendon health, mobility, nutrition, and recovery).

Assumptions:
- Meet squat, bench, deadlift: openers to 3 attempts on meet day (within single-day competition).
- Training days: 4 sessions per week (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat) during peak, with 1-2 lighter touch-ins as needed.
- Access: full gym, with ability to use accommodating resistance if desired (bands/chains optional, not required).
- Current numbers: you didn’t specify, so you’ll need to adjust loads using relative RPE and percentages for your lifter. Use a 1–2 RM test-if-needed approach only if you’re confident; otherwise use RPE-based autoregulation.

Goals of the 3-week peak:
- Week 1: 70–75% of perceived 1RM equivalent for competition lifts, but with high intent and long pauses/speed work; volume reduced by ~40–50% from peak training cycles.
- Week 2: Narrower windows, intensities increase to near 90–97% 1RM for singles/doubles, but total weekly volume stays low.
- Week 3 (taper week): Minimal volume, maximal freshness, meet day prep; priority on sleep, nutrition, mobility, and practise attempts.

Weekly structure:
- 4 training days: 
  - Day 1: Upper (bench emphasis)
  - Day 2: Lower (squat emphasis)
  - Day 3: Rest or light active recovery
  - Day 4: Upper (bench/deadlift accessory emphasis)
  - Day 5: Lower (deadlift emphasis)
  - Day 6–7: Rest or very light mobility

Note: Since it’s a 3-week taper, you can consolidate into 4 sessions per week as follows:
- Week 1 (Taper start): Wait to maintain familiarity with technique; still 4 sessions.
- Week 2: 3 sessions with one light day removed if needed.
- Week 3 (Meet week): 2 short sessions midweek plus rest leading to meet day.

Weeks 1–3: detailed plan

Week 1 (Taper begins, volume cut 40–50%, intensity at 70–75%)
Sessions:
- Day 1: Upper – Bench emphasis
  - Warm-up: mobility + shoulder prehab (band pull-aparts, dislocations) 5–7 min
  - Bench press: work up to 5 sets of 3 at 70–75% 1RM-equivalent (roughly RPE 7–8), aiming for fast but controlled reps with long pauses at chest (2-second pause). 3 reps x 5 sets? If you’re at 70–75% 1RM, do 4 sets of 4–5 reps or 5x3. For tempo, use 2-0-1-0 or 1-0-1-0 depending on control.
  - Close-grip bench (optional): 3x6 at 60–65% for bar speed and lockout.
  - Accessory work: 2–3 sets of 8–10 reps:
    - DB incline press or peace-keeper press (low weight, high quality)
    - Tricep pushdowns or skull crushers: 3x10
    - Band external rotations: 3x15
  - Core: 2x20 ab wheels or hanging leg raises.

- Day 2: Lower – Squat emphasis (quads, glutes)
  - Warm-up: hip ROM, ankle mobility, light movement prep
  - Back squat: 5x3 at 70–75% with explosive intent on the ascent; focus on bar speed and stable pelvis.
  - Paused goblet squat or paused front squat: 3x5 at 60–65% to maintain technique with a pause (2 seconds at bottom).
  - RDL or Hamstring work: 3x8–10
  - Leg extension: 3x12
  - Hamstring curls: 3x12
  - Core: 2x12-15 stability holds or planks

- Day 3: Rest or light cardio and mobility

- Day 4: Upper – Deadlift accessory emphasis
  - Warm-up: mobility
  - Deadlift: 2–3 sets of 3 at 70–75%? If competing standards use conventional or sumo, do 3x3 at 70–75% with a controlled tempo (2–0–1–0), pulling to knee height if flexibility is limited.
  - Rack pulls or block pulls: 3x4 at 70–75% for lockout strength
  - Barbell row: 3x8
  - Lat pulldown or pull-ups: 3x8–10
  - Face pulls: 3x15
  - CGBP (close-grip bench press): 3x6-8 to maintain triceps and lockout.

- Day 5: Lower – Deadlift emphasis
  - Warm-up: hip hinge practice
  - Deadlift: 4x2 at 70–75% with high speed on the first rep; aim for 2-second eccentric
  - Deficit deadlift or tempo deadlift: 3x4 at 60–65% (focus on hip hinge)
  - Bulgarian split squat: 3x8 per leg
  - Glute-ham raise or glute bridges: 3x12
  - Abs: 3x15 ab wheel or cable core

- Day 6–7: Rest or optional light mobility and light cardio 20–30 min

Weeks 2–3: progressive intensity, further volume reduction, maximize freshness

Week 2 (Taper continues, volume down 20–30%, intensity near 85–95%)
- Day 1: Upper – Bench intensity day
  - Bench: 3x2 at 85–90% (or RPE 8–9). Focus on bar speed and a clean touch-and-go or pause at chest for control (1 second pause)
  - Bench press variations: 2x2 at 90–92% (optional)
  - Accessory: 2x6 DB incline with moderate weight, 2x8 db rows, 2x12 lateral raises
  - Triceps: 2x8–10 dips or pushdowns

- Day 2: Lower – Squat emphasis
  - Squat: 3x2 at 85–90% with a fast concentric and controlled descent
  - Paused squat: 2x2 at 75–80% (2-second pause)
  - Hamstring work: 2x6–8
  - Core: 2x12 anti-rotation or farmer carry 2x40 seconds

- Day 3: Rest/Recovery
  - Light cardio 20–30 min, mobility, myofascial release

- Day 4: Upper – Combined bench/deadlift accessory
  - Deadlift: 2x2 at 85–90% if tolerated; otherwise 1x2
  - Barbell row: 3x6
  - Pull-ups/lat pulldown: 3x8
  - Overhead press: 3x6-8 for shoulder stability
  - Core: 2x12

- Day 5: Lower – Light deadlift emphasis
  - Deadlift: 2x2 at 75–80% (engineered for speed)
  - RDL: 3x6–8
  - Split squat with tempo: 3x6
  - Calf raises: 3x12
  - Core: 2x15

- Days 6–7: Rest or very light mobility work

Week 3 (Meet week): Taper to peak; minimal volume, max readiness; meet day is final performance
- Objective: maintain sharpness while ensuring fatigue is near zero; sleep, nutrition, and hydration are critical.

- Day 1: Upper light touch
  - Bench: 1x2 at 80% or less, 2–3 sets of 1–2 reps with fast bar speed
  - Accessory: 2x6–8 DB incline, 2x6–8 cable rows
  - Tricep: 2x8

- Day 2: Lower light touch
  - Squat: 1x2 at 80%, 1x1 at 85%, with near full recovery
  - Pause or tempo bottom squat: 1x2 at 75%
  - Light hamstring work: 2x8
  - Core: 1x12

- Day 3: Rest or mobility

- Day 4: Light upper
  - Bench: 1x1 at 85–90% with max speed
  - Rows: 2x6
  - Light accessory: 1–2 sets of 6–8

- Day 5: Rest and meet readiness check
  - Visualize attempts, technical cues, ensure nutrition plan ready

- Meet Day:
  - Warm-up: 20–30 minutes total (movement prep, activation, light speed sets)
  - Attempt structure: 
    - Squat: opener around 92–94% of projected max, second 97–99% if feel good, third attempt 100%+ if possible
    - Bench: similar plan; ensure grip width consistent; use opening around 90–92%
    - Deadlift: opener at or near 90%; second at 95–98% if energy allows; third attempt at 100%+ if successful
  - Nutrition: maintain hydration, small pre-meal that is easy to digest 1.5–2 hours pre-competition; carbohydrate focus around 2–3 g/kg total for the day if you’re accustomed; salt intake to maintain hydration.

Nutrition and recovery notes
- Sleep: target 8–9 hours per night during weeks 1–3; emphasize consistent bedtimes.
- Nutrition: maintain energy balance close to maintenance or slight surplus on heavy lifting days; ensure adequate protein 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day; carbohydrates around 3–5 g/kg/day depending on bodyweight and training load.
- Hydration: daily 30–40 ml/kg water; 500–750 ml extra around training; consider electrolyte balance if sweating heavily.
- Supplements: 
  - Creatine monohydrate 3–5 g/day to support strength and recovery
  - Caffeine strategically on meet day and high-intensity sessions (3–6 mg/kg 30–60 minutes pre-session)
  - Vitamin D3 and omega-3s if dietary intake is low
  - Multivitamin as needed

Notes on load and autoregulation
- If the athlete feels unusually fatigued or technique deteriorates, drop the load 5–10% and maintain reps with a focus on perfect form.
- Use RPE to guide sets: target RPE 7–8 for most sets during Week 1, RPE 8–9 for Week 2, RPE 9–10 only on meet-day-ready sets at 1–2 reps left in the tank.

Warm-up and technique
- Prioritize a dynamic warm-up with mobility for hips, shoulders, thoracic spine; 10–12 minutes before each session.
- Prior to main lifts, perform 2–3 sets of lighter warm-up sets (e.g., 40–60% for 3–5 reps) to dial in technique and bar speed.

Programming notes for adaptation
- If the lifter reports persistent soreness, reduce volume further and rely on technique-focused loads; emphasize mobility and tissue quality.
- If a lifter hits a new top single during Week 2 and feels strong, adjust the plan to include a single at 95–98% with full recovery between attempts.

Safety considerations
- Stop if pain is sharp, joint instability occurs, or technique breaks down significantly.
- Ensure spotters and safety equipment are ready on heavy sets.

The cardio is designed to support recovery, maintain movement quality, and aid passive fatigue management without compromising strength or nervous system readiness.

Principles for competition-day prep cardio
- Intensity: low to very low (RPE 3–4), easy conversational pace.
- Frequency: 3–4 short sessions across Weeks 1–3, with slightly more emphasis in Week 1 as fatigue-resilience builds.
- Modality: low-impact options that minimize muscle damage and preserve bar speed (e.g., brisk walks, stationary cycling, pool walking if available, light elliptical with resistance off).
- Duration: 15–25 minutes per session, never pushing toward voluntary fatigue.
- Timing: avoid cardio immediately before heavy lifting days; place on rest/recovery days or after lighter sessions if needed, ensuring at least 4–6 hours before any heavy lifting when possible.

Where to slot cardio in the 3-week plan
- Week 1 (taper start):
  - Add 2 short cardio sessions on non-lifting days or after light technique work, 15–20 minutes each at conversational pace.
  - If you have a light day (Day 3 or Day 6) you can add a 15-minute easy walk post-session to aid recovery.
- Week 2:
  - 1–2 optional 15–20 minute easy sessions on rest days or after the lighter upper/lower accessory days. Keep it very gentle; avoid any accumulation that could impact sleep or appetite.
- Week 3 (meet week):
  - 1 very light session early in the week (e.g., Monday) 15 minutes at an easy pace as a “movement priming” session. Do not do cardio on meet day or within 6–8 hours of any lifting attempts.
  - If you’re sensation-light and well-rested, a 10-minute mobility walk later in the week may be acceptable, but keep it minimal.

Sample competition-day prep cardio prescriptions (examples you can mirror)
- Week 1:
  - Cardio A: 20 minutes brisk walk outdoors or on treadmill at 4–5 METs, shoes on, arms relaxed. Focus on diaphragmatic breathing and cadence dance of steps.
  - Cardio B: 15 minutes easy stationary bike, resistance 0–1, cadence comfortable (no high RPM), avoid interval work.
- Week 2:
  - Cardio A: 15–20 minutes easy walk or bike, same RPE target; optional 5 minutes of light pool walking if available (gentle).
- Week 3:
  - Cardio A: 10–15 minutes easy walk or bike early in the week, no cardio within 6–8 hours of any training session that week. If you must, keep it under 10 minutes and very easy.

Adjustments and notes
- If the lifter reports trouble sleeping or appetite changes, scale back the cardio to 1 session per week, or reduce duration to 10–15 minutes at an even lower intensity.
- The cardio should not replace any of the dedicated recovery modalities (sleep, nutrition, hydration, mobility work). It complements them.
- If the client has any joint issues (knees, hips, back), prioritize non-impact options (elliptical with no incline, bike) and avoid positions that provoke pain.
- Consider wearables or rate-of-perceived-exertion monitoring to ensure strict adherence to low-intensity zones.

Safety reminders

- Hydration and nutrition around cardio sessions should be consistent with daily needs; do not overcompensate with extra calories solely to cover cardio.

Great question. In a peaking block, you want to balance consistent technique with minimizing fatigue and cognitive load. Here’s a practical approach for the shoulder cue you described.

Context
- Pinning the shoulder blades together (retraction) vs. allowing a bit of scapular movement can influence bar path, chest position, and tricep activation on bench.
- In early training you may cue different scapular positions; in a peak you want stable, repeatable technique that transfers to competition.

Recommendation
- Keep a simple, consistent cue you can reliably reproduce under fatigue. If “pull shoulders together” is the cue she can consistently execute with good bar path and chest up, keep it.
- If you observe that the cue creates excessive upper-back tension or rib flare, or disrupts rhythm, simplify further to one primary cue that aligns with competition technique.

Practical plan for the 3-week peak
- Week 1 (taper start): Use the shoulders-together cue as the primary bench cue during all work sets. Reinforce with a secondary cue only if needed to fix a specific issue (e.g., “brim chest up” or “elbows tucked to ribcage”). Don’t introduce new cues that require extra neuromuscular work.
- Week 2: Maintain the same primary cue. If technique begins to waver on higher-intensity work, use a micro-cue correction during warm-ups only (e.g., “pause at chest, maintain scapular set for 1 rep”). Avoid constant cue-switching.
- Week 3 (meet week): Prioritize automaticity. The cue should be internalized enough that she can reproduce it with minimal cognitive load. If she’s clean in practice with shoulders retracted, no new cues. If she’s off, revert to a very simple, rate-limited reminder (e.g., “tight chest, stable shoulders”) rather than technical overhauls.

Implementation tips
- Dry-run with light sets: 2–3 sets of 3 at slow tempo focusing on shoulder position, then return to competition pace.
- Use cue cards or a one-word cue for tempo during meet week (e.g., “Set!” or “Tight”).
- Monitor for shoulder health: if cueing creates excessive tension or aggravated deltoids/RC issues, ease up on retraction intensity and emphasize scapular stability and flat back position rather than extreme retraction.
- Video check: 1 short video snapshot per week to confirm the shoulder position and bar path remain consistent.

Decide if you should drill or leave as is
- If the lifter’s bench requires a consistent upper-back position and chest elevation to optimize bar path and arch, drill the cue briefly (2–3 focused reps at light load) during warm-ups in Week 1, then rely on it without heavy drilling in Weeks 2–3.
- If the cue is already working and adds no fatigue, keep it. Only add brief, targeted corrections if a drift is observed on higher-intensity work.

Bottom line
- Use a single, reliable cue for the peaking block. If “pull shoulders together” helps, keep it and reinforce throughout Week 1; reduce cue density in Weeks 2–3 to maintain peak freshness and automaticity. If it starts to create tension or disrupt tempo, simplify to a calmer cue and ensure scapular stability rather than aggressive retraction. Here’s a practical, competition-day morning plan for the meet-day routine. It focuses on minimizing fatigue, ensuring consistent technique, and allowing a smooth progression from wakefulness to attempting lifts. It’s written as a step-by-step timeline you can hand to your athlete or adapt to the meet’s schedule.

Overall philosophy
- Sleep and digestion: The plan assumes normal sleep the night before; try to wake with enough time to execute the routine without rushing. If the meet has a later start, you’ll still use the same sequence but with a longer buffer.
- Warm-up intensity: Keep the warm-up brisk but non-fatiguing. Prioritize mobility, activation, technique, and bar speed on warm-ups, not loaded single-rep max efforts.
- Attempt sequencing: Openers are chosen to feel confident but not maximal; second attempts are closer to meet plan; third attempts are contingent on feel and energy.

Sample morning-of meet-day routine (timeline)
06:30–07:00: Wake and initial readiness
- Light hydration: 250–350 ml water with a small pinch of salt if you sweat heavily the day prior (keep fluids consistent with routine).
- Morning movement: 5–8 minutes of very light movement (ankle circles, hip openers, thoracic rotations) to wake the system without fatigue.
- Breakfast: Easy-to-digest meal 60–90 minutes before warm-ups (examples: oatmeal with banana and honey, rice porridge, or toast with jam and a bit of peanut butter). 40–60 g carbohydrates, moderate protein, low fat and fiber to minimize GI distress.
- Caffeine: If she normally uses caffeine, take the usual dose 30–45 minutes before warm-ups. If not, avoid introducing a new stimulant.

07:00–07:30: Competition warm-up window begins
- Mobility and activation (5–8 minutes):
  - Shoulder circles, band pull-aparts, scapular push-ups
  - Hip openers (90/90 hip rocks), ankle dorsiflexion, thoracic spine mobilizations
- General bodyweight warm-up (3–5 minutes): light locomotion, bodyweight squats or inchworms, light push-ups

07:30–08:15: First lifting warm-ups (lifts executed as per meet lineup)
- Squat warm-up sequence (if squat is first to attempt)
  - Bar only (20–30 seconds)
  - 40 kg (10–15 seconds between)
  - 60 kg, 70 kg, etc., ramping to opening attempt
  - For each heavier step: 2–3 reps each, pausing briefly to ensure technique and depth
- Bench warm-up sequence (if bench is first or second)
  - Bar only
 40–60 kg as appropriate, then progressing to 60–80% for a couple of triples or doubles
- Deadlift warm-up sequence (if deadlift is last)
  - Bar only, then light sets at 60–70%, increasing toward opening attempt

Opening attempts and warm-up timing
- Opening attempts are typically set to be available about 60–90 minutes after waking up, depending on meet schedule. The key is that the lifter has completed all warm-ups and has a clear plan for the first attempt well before going on stage.
- Example progression (adjust based on actual opener numbers and federation rules):
  - Bench: Open around 88–92% of projected opener
  - Squat: Open around 92–94% of projected opener
  - Deadlift: Open around 90–93% of projected opener
- Ensure the lifter has a single, confident rhythm per lift: light warm-ups, a single heavy warm-up set to check bar speed, then the opener.

12–15 minutes between attempts
- After each attempt, perform a quick post-lift check:
  - Re-tidy grip, reset shoulders, ensure stable hip position
  - Light breathing drill to reset CNS (diaphragmatic breathing 4–6 breaths)
  - If the first attempt is solid, proceed to next warm-up quickly; if a technical issue arises, take an extra light attempt or a technical correction as appropriate.

Accessory maintenance and injury care (optional, not fatigue-inducing)
- Small, non-fatiguing maintenance movements: banded mobility to maintain shoulder and hip position, very light core activation, no additional sets to failure.
- If pre-existing minor niggles arise, address with light soft tissue work and targeted mobility (5–7 minutes total) rather than heavy rehab work.

Here’s a concise, end-to-end summary of the full 3-week meet-prep block, including workouts, the deload between Week 1 and Week 2, Week 2’s 95% singles, Week 3 taper, and the meet-day plan (with competition-day prep cardio integrated). It’s written as a clear, at-a-glance roadmap you can hand to your athlete or use to quickly check progression.

Overall structure
- Total duration: 3 weeks of peak, with a 4–5 day deload inserted between Week 1 and Week 2 to reset CNS and tissue readiness.
- Lifts emphasized: Squat, bench, deadlift (competition-style openers on meet day).
- Training days: 4 sessions per week during Weeks 1–3 (adjusted to maintain technique and freshness during the peak).

Week 1: Taper start (70–75% intensity, volume reduced 40–50%)
- Goals: Maintain technique and bar speed, begin fatigue management, set up deload for Week 2.
- Sample structure (4 lifting days):
  - Bench: 5x3 at 70–75% or 4–5x4; focus on fast, controlled reps with a 2-second pause at chest.
  - Squat: 5x3 at 70–75% with explosive ascent; paused variants 3x5 at 60–65%.
  - Deadlift: 2–3 sets of 3 at 70–75%; accessory pulls (rack/block pulls) 3x4.
  - Accessories: 2–3 sets of 8–12 (light); core work.
- Optional cardio: 15–20 minutes easy, non-fatiguing.
- Deload prep: Plan the deload slot; begin to reduce CNS load and ensure movement quality.

Deload (4–5 days) between Week 1 and Week 2
- Purpose: Tissue recovery, CNS reset, technique clean-up, movement pattern maintenance with minimal fatigue.
- Structure (3–4 light sessions total):
  - Upper: 3x4 at 50–60% with tight pauses; emphasize scapular retraction and chest-up.
  - Lower: 3x4 paused at bottom or tempo squats at 50–60%.
  - Mobility: 10–15 minutes focusing on shoulders, hips, ankles.
  - Optional light cardio: 15–20 minutes once if recovered.
- Intensity: Keep RPE around 5–6; no maximal or near-max attempts.
- Note: If tissue sensitivity is higher or CNS fatigue persists, shorten deload to 3 days or compress into lighter sessions with more emphasis on technique.

Week 2: Return to peak with 95% singles (low volume)
- Goals: Confirm readiness with 95% singles; maintain technique; minimal fatigue.
- Structure (4 sessions):
  - Bench emphasis with 95% single: 1x at 95% (projected opener); rest 4–5 minutes; if needed, scale to 92–93%.
  - Squat emphasis with 95% single: 1x at 95% opener projection; 4–6 minutes rest; ensure depth and bar path.
  - Deadlift emphasis with 95% single: 1x at 95%; 4–6 minutes rest.
  - Light technique/density work: 2–3 sets of 2–3 reps at 75–80% to keep groove; accessory work 2–3 sets of 8–10.
  - Optional light day: Rest or very light mobility day.
- Cardio: If used, keep it very light (15–20 minutes) and non-fatiguing on recovery days only.
- Notes: If any lift shows technique breakdown or signs of fatigue, back off the percentage to 90–92% for the single or shift to a more conservative week plan.

Week 3: Meet-week taper and freshness
- Goals: Maximal readiness; minimal fatigue; automatic technique; sleep and nutrition primed.
- Structure (2–4 short sessions total, depending on meet schedule):
  - Light technique sessions per lift: 1–2 sets of 2 at 80–85%, then 1x1 at 70–75% as feel allows.
  - Very low volume and intensity leading into meet day; no fatigue-inducing work.
- Warm-ups: Prioritize dynamic warm-up, mobility, activation, and rehearsal of cues (shoulder retraction cue on bench, brace on squats, hip hinge and bar path on deadlift).
- Meet-day prep cardio: Optional very light movement on non-meet days (15 minutes max) and no cardio on meet day.
- Sleep and recovery: Optimize sleep (8–9 hours), keep caffeine timing consistent with routine, nutrition to sustain energy.

Meet-day plan (condensed)
- Morning routine: wake, mobility, light activation, breakfast 60–90 minutes pre-warmups, caffeine if habitual.
- Warm-ups: Graduated, quick ramp to opening attempts; ensure a consistent rhythm for all three lifts.
- Attempt structure: Openers around a safe, confident percentage (bench ~88–92% of projected opener, squat ~92–94%, deadlift ~90–93%), then second attempts closer to plan, third attempts as energy allows.
- Recovery between attempts: 4–6 minutes for bigger lifts; diaphragmatic breathing to reset.
- Nutrition: steady hydration with electrolytes; 1.5–2.5 g/kg carbohydrate in the 3–4 hours pre-lift window; small sips between attempts if energy dips; easy-to-digest meals pre-event to minimize GI distress.
- Post-lift: light mobility and breathing reset; protein-rich snack within 30–60 minutes.

General nutrition and recovery notes (throughout the 3 weeks)
- Protein: 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day, distributed across meals.
- Carbohydrates: 4–6 g/kg/day (adjust up if training load was higher or glycogen depleted).
- Fats: moderate; avoid large fat meals extremely close to lifts to minimize GI distress.
- Hydration: baseline 30–35 ml/kg/day; additional around training; electrolyte management based on sweat rate and environment.
- Sleep: target 8–9 hours per night; prioritize consistency and sleep hygiene.
- Supplements: creatine 3–5 g/day; caffeine strategically on meet day/morning; vitamin D3 and omega-3s if needed; multivitamin as needed.

Compensation and autoregulation
- If fatigue or technique deteriorates, reduce loads 5–10% while maintaining reps to preserve form.
- Use RPE targets: Week 1 sets around RPE 7–8, Week 2 around RPE 8–9 for singles, Week 3 near 9–10 only for near-max efforts on warm-ups or the (optional) 95% singles if retained.
- If adjustments are needed due to schedule or fatigue, shift the deload, reduce volume further in Week 2, or rearrange 95% singles to Week 1 end if necessary.
